title: Proposition 16.13.3 (Strict compact stability with zero spectral bottom)
search_title: Strict compact stability with zero spectral bottom
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Proposition 16.13.3 (Strict compact stability with zero spectral bottom) . 7B9E16310EBB For every nonzero $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ the grim-reaper form satisfies \[  Q_ v(\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\operatorname {sech}s\,  |(\phi \cosh s)'|^2ds>0.  \] Nevertheless its variational spectral bottom is \[  \inf _{0\ne \phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)} \frac{Q_ v(\phi )}{\int \phi ^2\cosh s\, ds}=0.  \] Proof Insert $w=\operatorname {sech}s$ in Proposition 14.14.6 to get the formula. Equality would make $\phi \cosh s$ constant; compact support forces that constant to be zero. To compute the infimum, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi $ equal to one on $[-1,1]$, supported in $[-2,2]$, and put $\phi _ R=w\chi (s/R)$. Then \[  Q_ v(\phi _ R)=R^{-2}\int \operatorname {sech}s\, |\chi '(s/R)|^2ds \le R^{-2}\| \chi '\| _\infty ^2\pi ,  \] while $\int \phi _ R^2\rho _ v\to \pi $ by dominated convergence. Stability gives the opposite bound zero. The null function $w$ in the weighted square-integrable kernel is not compactly supported, so there is no contradiction with strict positivity on compact tests. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.13.4 (A one-dimensional Schrödinger form)
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Proposition 16.13.4 (A one-dimensional Schrödinger form) . 752E1E7B14D3 The substitution $\psi =\sqrt{\cosh s}\, \phi $ preserves the weighted $L^2$ norm and transforms the grim-reaper quadratic form into \[  Q_ v(\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\left[|\psi '|^2+ \left(\frac14-\frac34\operatorname {sech}^2s\right)\psi ^2\right]ds  \] for compactly supported smooth real tests. The weighted null field $\operatorname {sech}s$ becomes $\operatorname {sech}^{1/2}s$. Proof Writing $h=\log \cosh s$ gives $\phi =e^{-h/2}\psi $. Thus the weighted derivative energy is $\int (\psi '-h'\psi /2)^2$. Integrate the cross term by parts; its contribution is $h''\psi ^2/2$. The resulting potential for the full quadratic form is $h''/2+(h')^2/4-|A|^2$. Substituting $h''=\operatorname {sech}^2s$, $(h')^2=1-\operatorname {sech}^2s$ and $|A|^2=\operatorname {sech}^2s$ gives the formula. The norm identity and the transformed null field follow immediately from the substitution. No complete spectral resolution is asserted. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.13.5 (Grim cylinders have a different square-integrable kernel)
search_title: Grim cylinders have a different square-integrable kernel
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Proposition 16.13.5 (Grim cylinders have a different square-integrable kernel) . 01561F6C5365 Let $M$ be the product of the complete unit grim reaper with $\mathbb R^ k$, $k\ge 1$, translating in its grim-reaper plane. It is weighted stable and has variational spectral bottom zero, but it has no nonzero smooth Jacobi field in $L^2(\rho _ vdA)$. Proof The metric is $ds^2+|dy|^2$, the weight is $\cosh s$, and the operator is the one in Proposition 16.13.1 plus $\Delta _ y$. The function $w(s,y)=\operatorname {sech}s$ is a positive Jacobi field, proving stability. It is not weighted square-integrable because its squared integral in $s$ is $\pi $ and the Euclidean factor has infinite volume. Lemma 14.14.10 therefore gives the zero kernel. For the spectral bottom, multiply the cutoff tests of Proposition 16.13.3 by $\eta (y/R)$, with nonzero smooth compactly supported $\eta $ on $\mathbb R^ k$. Separation of variables makes the Rayleigh quotient the sum of the grim-reaper quotient and $R^{-2}\int |\nabla \eta |^2/\int \eta ^2$. Both tend to zero. This example has zero infimum without a nonzero weighted square-integrable null field; it does not require an assertion about the entire spectrum. $\square$

title: Example 16.13.6 (A translating plane has a positive weighted gradient gap)
search_title: A translating plane has a positive weighted gradient gap
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Example 16.13.6 (A translating plane has a positive weighted gradient gap) . 84BE9F6FEFFB Let $P\cong \mathbb R^ n$ be an affine hyperplane and let $0\ne v$ be tangent to it. The image is stationary under translation by $v$, but its translator-weighted form has variational spectral bottom $|v|^2/4$. Its induced Euclidean metric is complete and its induced conformal translator metric is incomplete. Proof Since $A=0$, the Jacobi form equals the weighted gradient energy. For $\psi =e^{\langle x,v\rangle /2}\phi $, integration of the compactly supported cross term gives \[  Q_ v(\phi )=\int _ P\left(|\nabla \psi |^2+\frac{|v|^2}{4}\psi ^2\right)dA, \qquad \int _ P\phi ^2\rho _ v\, dA=\int _ P\psi ^2dA.  \] The lower bound is immediate. Taking $\psi _ R(x)=\eta ((x-p)/R)$ for a fixed nonzero compactly supported smooth $\eta $ makes its gradient Rayleigh quotient tend to zero, proving sharpness. Euclidean completeness is that of an affine plane. The ray $p-tv/|v|$ stays in $P$ and has finite conformal length by Proposition 14.15.1 , proving the final assertion. A tangential velocity changes this weighted functional even though it does not change the plane's image under the flow. $\square$

title: 5.7 Vector measures and the mass of a current
search_title: Vector measures and the mass of a current
section: 5.7 Vector measures and the mass of a current
text: The positive representation theorem extends to finite-dimensional vector-valued tests. We give the functional-analytic steps explicitly, including the passage from the comass of a form to the mass norm of a multivector. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Theorem 5.14, printed pp. 37–38, and Chapter 6, Remark 2.7 and equations (2.8)–(2.10), printed pp. 160–161. Simon initially uses the Euclidean norm; the argument below works for an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm. Completeness of the real spaces $L^1$ and $L^2$, elementary integration, and finite-dimensional norm duality are background inputs. Lemma 5.7.1 (Representation of a bounded functional on a real Hilbert space) . 63273388A3B5 If $\mathcal H$ is a real Hilbert space and $L:\mathcal H\to \mathbb R$ is bounded and linear, there is a unique $z\in \mathcal H$ with $L(x)=\langle x,z\rangle $ for all $x$. Moreover $\| z\| =\| L\| $. Proof The case $L=0$ is immediate. Otherwise the closed affine set $A=\{ x:L(x)=1\} $ is nonempty and its distance $d$ from zero is positive, since $1\leq \| L\| \| x\| $ on $A$. Choose $x_ j\in A$ with $\| x_ j\| \to d$. Their midpoints belong to $A$, so the parallelogram identity gives \[  \| x_ j-x_ k\| ^2=2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2-4\left\| \frac{x_ j+x_ k}{2}\right\| ^2 \leq 2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2-4d^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] Completeness gives a minimizer $x_0\in A$. For $y\in \ker L$, minimizing $\| x_0+ty\| ^2$ in $t$ yields $\langle x_0,y\rangle =0$. As $x-L(x)x_0\in \ker L$, we get $L(x)=\langle x,x_0\rangle /\| x_0\| ^2$. Set $z=x_0/\| x_0\| ^2$. Testing differences against themselves proves uniqueness. Cauchy–Schwarz and testing $z/\| z\| $ give the norm identity. $\square$ Proposition 5.7.2 (The dual of a sigma-finite real integration space) . A1288D51AB95 Let $(X,\mu )$ be a sigma-finite measure space. Every bounded linear functional $L:L^1(\mu ;\mathbb R)\to \mathbb R$ has the form \[  L(f)=\int _ X f\eta \, d\mu ,\qquad \eta \in L^\infty (\mu ),\qquad \| \eta \| _\infty =\| L\| .  \] The density $\eta $ is unique up to a null set. Proof Choose measurable $E_ j\uparrow X$ with $\mu (E_ j)<\infty $. Extending by zero gives a bounded restriction of $L$ to $L^2(E_ j)$, because $\| f\| _1\leq \mu (E_ j)^{1/2}\| f\| _2$. Lemma 5.7.1 gives a density $\eta _ j\in L^2(E_ j)$. Write $C=\| L\| $. If $F=\{ |\eta _ j|>C+\varepsilon \} \subset E_ j$ had positive measure, the $L^2$ test $\operatorname {sign}(\eta _ j)1_ F$ would imply \[  (C+\varepsilon )\mu (F)<\int _ F|\eta _ j|\, d\mu =L(\operatorname {sign}(\eta _ j)1_ F)\leq C\mu (F),  \] a contradiction. Thus $|\eta _ j|\leq C$ almost everywhere. On $E_ i\subset E_ j$, all $L^2(E_ i)$ tests give the same integral for $\eta _ i$ and $\eta _ j$; testing their difference proves agreement. Discarding countably many null sets glues the densities to $\eta $ on $X$. Truncating both the domain to $E_ j$ and the values of an arbitrary $f\in L^1$ approximates it in $L^1$ by bounded functions supported in finite-measure sets. Continuity proves the formula for every $f$. The norm equality follows from $\| \eta \| _\infty \leq C$ and $|L(f)|\leq \| \eta \| _\infty \| f\| _1$. Uniqueness follows by testing the sign of the difference on finite-measure subsets where its absolute value is bounded below. $\square$ Lemma 5.7.3 (The positive variation functional) . A217FEC406E3 Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ open, and $L:C_ c(U;E)\to \mathbb R$ linear. Suppose for each compact $K\subset U$ there is $C_ K<\infty $ with $|L(F)|\leq C_ K\| F\| _\infty $ whenever $\operatorname {spt}F\subset K$. For $g\in C_ c(U)$ with $g\geq 0$, put \[  \lambda (g)=\sup \{ |L(F)|:F\in C_ c(U;E),\  \| F(x)\| \leq g(x)\text{ for every }x\} .  \] Then $\lambda $ is additive and nonnegatively homogeneous on nonnegative functions. It extends uniquely to a positive linear functional on $C_ c(U)$. Proof The supremum is finite by the local bound and the support of $g$. Homogeneity is immediate. For additivity from below, choose almost maximizing tests for $g$ and $h$, reversing each sign so that its $L$-value is nonnegative. Their sum is admissible for $g+h$. For the reverse inequality, split any admissible $F$ as \[  F_1=\frac{g}{g+h}F,\qquad F_2=\frac{h}{g+h}F  \] where $g+h>0$, and set both fields to zero elsewhere. These extensions are continuous: $\| F_1\| \leq g$ and $\| F_2\| \leq h$ force continuity at every zero of $g+h$. Each is admissible for its corresponding function, so $|L(F)|\leq \lambda (g)+\lambda (h)$. This proves additivity. Define $\lambda (f)=\lambda (f^+)-\lambda (f^-)$; equality of two decompositions into differences of nonnegative functions follows by cross-adding and using additivity. Hence this extension is linear and positive. $\square$ Theorem 5.7.4 (Polar representation for finite-dimensional tests) . 458374FA534D Under the hypotheses of Lemma 5.7.3 , there are a Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$ and a measurable $\xi :U\to E^*$ such that \[  L(F)=\int _ U\langle F,\xi \rangle \, d\mu ,\qquad \| \xi \| _{E^*}=1\quad \mu \text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lambda (g)=\int _ Ug\, d\mu \quad (g\in C_ c(U),\  g\geq 0).  \] The measure is determined by $\lambda $, and the field is unique $\mu $-almost everywhere for this measure. See [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.14; its Hilbert-space statement is the Euclidean-norm special case. Proof Theorem 2.3.7 applied to $\lambda $ gives $\mu $. In particular \[  |L(F)|\leq \lambda (\| F\| )=\int _ U\| F\| \, d\mu .  \] Choose a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ d$ of unit vectors of $E$. Each scalar functional $f\mapsto L(fe_ i)$ is bounded for the $L^1(\mu )$ norm. The density theorem 2.3.8 extends it uniquely from $C_ c(U)$ to $L^1(\mu )$. The measure is sigma-finite, since $U$ has a countable compact exhaustion and $\mu $ is finite on compacts. Proposition 5.7.2 gives coordinate densities $\eta _ i$. Define $\xi $ by $\langle e_ i,\xi \rangle =\eta _ i$. Finite linear expansion of $F$ proves the integral formula. For a fixed $q\in E$, the same domination applied to $fq$ and $L^1$ density give $|\langle q,\xi \rangle |\leq \| q\| $ almost everywhere. Take a countable dense subset of the unit ball and discard the union of the associated null sets. Continuity in $q$ then gives $\| \xi \| _{E^*}\leq 1$ almost everywhere. For every nonnegative $g\in C_ c(U)$, each admissible test in the definition of $\lambda (g)$ satisfies \[  |L(F)|\leq \int _ Ug\| \xi \| _{E^*}\, d\mu .  \] Taking the supremum yields \[  \int _ Ug\, d\mu =\lambda (g)\leq \int _ Ug\| \xi \| _{E^*}\, d\mu \leq \int _ Ug\, d\mu .  \] Consequently $\int g(1-\| \xi \| _{E^*})\, d\mu =0$ for every such $g$. Cutoffs equal to one on a compact exhaustion show that this nonnegative integrand vanishes almost everywhere. Positive Riesz uniqueness determines $\mu $, and scalar $L^1$ density determines each coordinate of $\xi $ uniquely. $\square$ Lemma 5.7.5 (Extending a finite-mass current to continuous forms) . CC6436C139E1 A current $T$ with locally finite mass on $U$ has a unique extension to compactly supported continuous $m$-forms that is bounded for uniform comass on each fixed compact support. For open $W\subset U$, its mass $\mathbf M_ W(T)$ is also the supremum of $|T(\omega )|$ over continuous compactly supported forms in $W$ of comass at most one. Proof Extend a continuous compactly supported form by zero and convolve its coefficients with smooth mollifiers of radii tending to zero. The resulting smooth forms converge uniformly; all sufficiently late supports lie in a common relatively compact open $V\subset U$. The mass bound makes their $T$-values Cauchy. The same estimate applied to the difference of any two approximating sequences proves independence. It also proves continuity and uniqueness of the extension. If the original support lies in $W$, choose the mollifier radii so the approximating supports also lie in $W$. Uniform approximation in the finite-dimensional comass norm gives upper bounds $1+\varepsilon _ j$ for the approximating comasses; divide by $1+\varepsilon _ j$ to obtain admissible smooth tests. Thus allowing continuous tests does not change the supremum. This is the extension preceding [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.8), with comass in place of the Euclidean norm. $\square$ Proposition 5.7.6 (Open-set mass from the positive variation functional) . F553EACEBF96 Apply Theorem 5.7.4 to the continuous extension of a locally finite-mass $m$-current, with $E=\Lambda ^ m(\mathbb R^ N)^*$ carrying comass. Its measure satisfies $\mu (W)=\mathbf M_ W(T)$ for every open $W\subset U$. The dual field has mass norm one almost everywhere and need not be simple. Proof For a continuous test supported in $W$ with comass at most one, the polar representation gives $|T(\omega )|\leq \mu (W)$. Conversely, if $0\leq g\leq 1$ has compact support in $W$, every test for $\lambda (g)$ is such a continuous mass test. Hence $\mathbf M_ W(T)\geq \lambda (g)=\int g\, d\mu $. Taking the supremum over these scalar cutoffs gives $\mu (W)$ by Radon regularity, including when it is infinite. The mass norm is precisely the dual of comass, so the unit-norm assertion follows from the vector representation theorem. Nothing in that theorem imposes decomposability of the polar multivector. $\square$

title: 16.14 A normal current without rectifiability
text: Normality controls a current and its boundary by measures, but does not force its mass to lie on a set of its own dimension. The following elementary example also makes visible the distinction between Euclidean and mass norms in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Remark 2.7, printed p. 160. Example 16.14.1 (A nonsimple bivector and its two norms) . 5584C114BE31 In oriented $\mathbb R^4$, put $\zeta =e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$. Its Euclidean norm is $\sqrt2$, while its mass norm is $2$. It is not simple. Proof The two basis bivectors are orthonormal, giving the Euclidean norm. Their individual mass norms are one, so the triangle inequality gives $|\zeta |_{\mathrm{mass}}\leq 2$. For the reverse inequality, let $\omega _0=dx^1\wedge dx^2+dx^3\wedge dx^4$. Define the orthogonal complex structure $Je_1=e_2$, $Je_2=-e_1$, $Je_3=e_4$, $Je_4=-e_3$. Then $\omega _0(u,v)=\langle Ju,v\rangle $, whose absolute value is at most one on orthonormal pairs. Equality holds at $(e_1,e_2)$, so $\omega _0$ has comass one. As $\langle \omega _0,\zeta \rangle =2$, duality gives the opposite mass bound. Finally $\zeta \wedge \zeta =2e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4\ne 0$, whereas the square of a simple bivector is zero. $\square$ Example 16.14.2 (A diffuse finite-mass two-current) . 4B74DFD48D85 Let $Q=[0,1]^4$ and define a two-current on $\mathbb R^4$ by \[  T(\omega )=\int _ Q\bigl (\omega _{12}(x)+\omega _{34}(x)\bigr )\, dx.  \] Then $\| T\| =2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$, its polar bivector is $\zeta /2$, and $\mathbf M(T)=2$. Its support is $Q$, and its mass measure is non-atomic. Proof The bound $|\langle \omega ,\zeta \rangle |\leq 2\| \omega \| _*$ shows that the formula is a current and bounds its mass by $2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$. For any open $W$ and any smooth scalar cutoff $0\leq g\leq 1$ compactly supported in $W$, the form $g\omega _0$ has comass at most one and $T(g\omega _0)=2\int _ Qg\, dx$. Taking the supremum of these cutoffs yields the reverse open-set mass bound. This identifies the measure and the polar field. Every ball about a point of $Q$ meets $Q$ in positive four-dimensional measure, while tests outside $Q$ vanish; hence the support is $Q$. Singletons have zero Lebesgue measure. $\square$ Proposition 16.14.3 (The diffuse current has a finite-mass boundary) . 852428C98493 The current in Example 16.14.2 is normal and satisfies $\mathbf M(\partial T)\leq 8$. title: Example 16.14.1 (A nonsimple bivector and its two norms)

text: Example 16.14.1 (A nonsimple bivector and its two norms) . 5584C114BE31 In oriented $\mathbb R^4$, put $\zeta =e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$. Its Euclidean norm is $\sqrt2$, while its mass norm is $2$. It is not simple. Proof The two basis bivectors are orthonormal, giving the Euclidean norm. Their individual mass norms are one, so the triangle inequality gives $|\zeta |_{\mathrm{mass}}\leq 2$. For the reverse inequality, let $\omega _0=dx^1\wedge dx^2+dx^3\wedge dx^4$. Define the orthogonal complex structure $Je_1=e_2$, $Je_2=-e_1$, $Je_3=e_4$, $Je_4=-e_3$. Then $\omega _0(u,v)=\langle Ju,v\rangle $, whose absolute value is at most one on orthonormal pairs. Equality holds at $(e_1,e_2)$, so $\omega _0$ has comass one. As $\langle \omega _0,\zeta \rangle =2$, duality gives the opposite mass bound. Finally $\zeta \wedge \zeta =2e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4\ne 0$, whereas the square of a simple bivector is zero. $\square$

title: Example 16.14.2 (A diffuse finite-mass two-current)
text: Example 16.14.2 (A diffuse finite-mass two-current) . 4B74DFD48D85 Let $Q=[0,1]^4$ and define a two-current on $\mathbb R^4$ by \[  T(\omega )=\int _ Q\bigl (\omega _{12}(x)+\omega _{34}(x)\bigr )\, dx.  \] Then $\| T\| =2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$, its polar bivector is $\zeta /2$, and $\mathbf M(T)=2$. Its support is $Q$, and its mass measure is non-atomic. Proof The bound $|\langle \omega ,\zeta \rangle |\leq 2\| \omega \| _*$ shows that the formula is a current and bounds its mass by $2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$. For any open $W$ and any smooth scalar cutoff $0\leq g\leq 1$ compactly supported in $W$, the form $g\omega _0$ has comass at most one and $T(g\omega _0)=2\int _ Qg\, dx$. Taking the supremum of these cutoffs yields the reverse open-set mass bound. This identifies the measure and the polar field. Every ball about a point of $Q$ meets $Q$ in positive four-dimensional measure, while tests outside $Q$ vanish; hence the support is $Q$. Singletons have zero Lebesgue measure. $\square$
